objects.text: Is it worth doing, and what would change my mind?

Applied AI and Automation  |  Session 11 of 12
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes:
Welcome back. Start with your question from last time: what would your chosen route cost in the first year, in hours and in shillings?

Today you answer it, and then ask the bigger question: is this task worth automating, in shillings?

You will build a costed case from the numbers you measured in Session 8, and you will write down what would change your mind.

title.text: Your two hours: 45 minutes are your own work

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_plan_11.90x3.95_2909979a.png
objects.alt: The two hours in parts, in minutes

objects.text: 45 of the 120 minutes are yours: your numbers, your costs, your decision.

slides.notes:
Three parts take most of the time. Twenty-five minutes of ideas on costs, benefits, the haircut, the three scenarios and stop rules. Twenty minutes where I fill the workbook live with the Nile Valley Foods numbers. After the break you have forty-five minutes on your own task, in three blocks of fifteen minutes.

The last ten minutes are for your decision: go, revise or stop.

runs.text: 1.  Name three things you ask a vendor before you sign.
2.  What are the three routes when you need a capability?
3.  A proposal promises industry-leading accuracy. What do you ask for?

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_question_2.80.png

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 10. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. Name three things you ask a vendor before you sign. Take a moment.

A good answer is this. Any three of: where the data is stored and who can see it; whether it trains on your data; renewal terms and a price cap; how you exit and get your data back; references; a monthly usage cap; who carries the exchange-rate risk.

Question two. What are the three routes when you need a capability? Say it to yourself first.

A good answer is this. Build it yourself, buy it, or partner with someone.

Question three. A proposal promises industry-leading accuracy. What do you ask for? Think about your own task as you answer.

A good answer is this. A measured error rate on documents like yours, and your own test on a sample.

If an answer was missing, your own task card or last workbook page has it. Now to today.

slides.notes:
Five words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Payback. The number of months the monthly net takes to repay the one-off cost.

Loaded hourly cost. Pay plus employer contributions and benefits, divided by hours worked. It is what an hour of staff time costs the company.

Haircut. The share of the benefit you choose not to count, because estimates are rarely exact.

Sensitivity. Trying a low, base and high version of your numbers to see whether the answer changes.

Stop rule. A number written in advance that tells you to stop or revise.

title.text:
A business case turns your
measured test into money

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_flow_11.90x3.90_fab666c3.png
objects.alt: A business case turns your measured test into money

objects.text: You already hold the first two steps. Today you add the money.

slides.notes:
Today's question is whether the task is worth doing and what would change your mind. A business case takes two things you already hold: the baseline from Session 1 and the measured test from Session 8. We put money on both sides: costs, benefits and payback, then a haircut for risk, then stop rules.

Why bother?

Gartner forecasts that over 40% of agent projects will be cancelled by 2027. That is a forecast for large global firms, and one commonly cited reason is unclear value. A short, honest case is the answer to that. It does not need to be perfect. Tell me now which number you are least sure of.

objects.text: Hours cost UGX 30,000 each (NVF figure, invented). If you buy, use the vendor's first-year total.

slides.notes:
These are the cost lines in the workbook, with the Nile Valley Foods figures. Licences each month. Set-up and training once. Review time every month: four runs of twenty minutes. It never goes away, so never set it to zero. Total: UGX 480,000 once and UGX 145,000 each month.

Hours use the loaded hourly cost: pay plus employer contributions and benefits, divided by hours worked. For example, UGX 4,500,000 a month plus UGX 500,000 is UGX 5,000,000, and over 160 hours that is about UGX 31,250 an hour. NVF rounds to UGX 30,000. If you buy or partner, put the vendor's first-year total in these lines.

title.text:
Benefits: count what you
measured, and write down the rest

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_bars_7.70x4.80_b1cd2d5f.png
objects.alt: Benefits: count what you measured, and write down the rest

objects.text: Count hours and errors. State the rest, and count it at zero.

runs.text: Hours: 4 runs x 85 minutes x UGX 30,000 an hour.
Errors: 4 runs x 40% x 60% removed x UGX 150,000.
Faster replies: write it, count 0.

slides.notes:
Benefits come from your measured test. Time saved is the runs a month, times the minutes saved before review, times the hourly cost. At NVF that is 4 runs times 85 minutes, which is 5.7 hours, at UGX 30,000 an hour: UGX 170,000 a month. Errors avoided is runs, times the error rate, times the share removed, times the cost of one error.

At NVF that is 4 runs, times 40 percent, times 60 percent, times UGX 150,000: UGX 144,000. Faster response and goodwill are real, but I write them down and count them at zero unless you can show a number. Benefit of UGX 314,000 less cost of 145,000 leaves UGX 169,000 a month.

title.text:
Worked example: the Monday
sales email pays back in 2.8 months

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_versus_7.70x4.80_0c55f79f.png
objects.alt: Worked example: the Monday sales email pays back in 2.8 months

objects.text: NVF (fictional), 4 runs a month, planned numbers.

runs.text: Monthly net: UGX 169,000.
12-month net: UGX 1,548,000.
After a 30% haircut: UGX 417,600.

slides.notes:
The finished NVF example, as in the workbook. By hand, 90 minutes. Planned with the automation, 5 to start and 20 to review, so 25. That saves 65 minutes a run after review. The workbook counts 85 minutes saved before review, then charges the 20 review minutes as a cost.

Net, that is the same 65 you measured. Benefit of UGX 314,000 less cost of UGX 145,000 leaves a monthly net of UGX 169,000. The one-off cost of UGX 480,000 divided by 169,000 is 2.8 months. Twelve months net of the one-off cost: UGX 1,548,000. With a 30 percent haircut: UGX 417,600.

These are planned numbers, and Session 12 shows how they compare with twelve real runs.

title.text:
A haircut shows how much
bad luck the case can survive

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_bars_7.70x4.80_c7f2670a.png
objects.alt: A haircut shows how much bad luck the case can survive

objects.text: Ask how much of the benefit can vanish before the case breaks.

runs.text: The haircut is a share you do not count.
Break-even haircut at NVF: about 41%.
Below zero: improve it, or wait.

slides.notes:
A haircut is how I stay honest. Estimates are rarely exact, so I choose a share of the benefit not to count. NVF uses thirty percent, which leaves UGX 417,600 over twelve months. The workbook also shows the break-even haircut: the point where the twelve month net reaches zero.

For NVF it is about forty-one percent. That gives the owner of the business a plain sentence: the case holds even if more than a third of the benefit never appears. If your break-even is small, your case is fragile. Thirty percent is a common starting point. Choose your own figure and explain it.

title.text:
Low, base and high: NVF is positive
in two cases and negative in one

rows.text: Volume 70%, saving 60%, errors avoided 40%, costs 30% higher
The numbers on your Inputs sheet

objects.text: Takeaway: a case that is positive in only two of three scenarios needs a stop rule for the low case.

slides.notes:
This is the Sensitivity sheet with the workbook's default factors. The monthly net is minus UGX 76,780 in the low case, UGX 169,000 in the base case and UGX 283,980 in the high case. In the low case, volume is seventy percent, only sixty percent of the saving happens, only forty percent of errors are removed, and costs are thirty percent higher.

The result is no payback. In the high case it pays back in about a month and a half. The haircut shrinks the benefit; sensitivity changes the assumptions. Use both. NVF is positive in two of three scenarios, so I ask what would have to be true in the low case, and I write it as a stop rule.

title.text: Write your stop rules before you start, as numbers

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_cross_0.70.png

objects.text: Stop if one error reaches a customer or the bank, until the cause is fixed.

objects.text: Revise if review minutes rise above 30 a run.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_chart_0.70.png

objects.text: Revise if the 12-month net after the haircut turns negative.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_calendar_0.70.png

objects.text: Stop if the saving is under half the plan after four weeks.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_check_0.70.png

objects.text: Scale only after the base case holds for two months.

slides.notes:
What would change my mind?

Write it down now, while you are calm. These are example rules for NVF. Stop if one error reaches a customer or the bank. Revise if review minutes climb above thirty a run. Revise if the twelve month net after the haircut turns negative. Stop if the saving after four weeks is under half the plan.

Scale only after the base case holds for two months. Each rule is a number somebody can check. In Session 12 these rules become your day 60 review test, so choose numbers you can read from your own Results Tracker.

title.text:
People decide whether the
automation succeeds: six plain steps

objects.text: Say what the saved time is for, so jobs feel safe.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_phone_0.69.png

objects.text: Give staff one place to report problems.

slides.notes:
A good business case can still fail because of people. Tell staff early what is coming and why. Train the people who check the results first, because their review time is in your costs. Name one owner, the person accountable for the automation, who holds the off switch.

Say clearly what the saved time is for, for example more customer visits or fewer late nights, so people do not fear for their jobs. Give everyone who uses the tool basic AI literacy. And give staff one place, a person or a shared inbox, to report problems.

Write these into the summary. Now I fill the workbook live so you can see the whole case in one place.

title.text: Decision: go, revise or stop for your own task?

objects.text: What do you decide, and which number decided it?

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_check_0.80.png

objects.text: Go
Positive after the haircut and in at least two scenarios. Start a limited pilot with a review date.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_gear_0.80.png

objects.text: Revise
Positive only in the base case. Fix the weakest number: review time, error cost or price.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_cross_0.80.png

objects.text: Stop
Negative after the haircut and in every case. Keep the workbook and retest when a number changes.
Write the decision and the one number that decided it on the summary page.

slides.notes:
Time to decide. Go means the case is positive after the haircut and in at least two of the three scenarios. Start a limited pilot with a review date. Revise means it is positive only in the base case, so fix the weakest number: review time, error cost or the tool price.

Stop means it is negative after the haircut, so keep the workbook and test again when a number changes. A stop with a clear reason also saves money. Write your decision and the one number that decided it. That number is what you lead with in Session 12.

Save the workbook and the summary page in the same folder as your task card and test log. Next session is demo day. You present your task, your result and your business case in eight minutes, so bring the workbook and one slide or page that shows the numbers.

Optional, if you want a head start: write down the one number that would make your sponsor say yes or no. That is your question for Session 12.

We began with this question: Is it worth doing, and what would change my mind? Before you go, say in one sentence what you can now say about it.
